prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and opening new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I keep B001 first after reading all eight ballots, and it is the only candidate that seven of eight members rank at all, with four first places. The discovery is physical, not only technical: trapping many atoms at the magic wavelength, where the light shift cancels, removes Doppler and recoil shifts, and once the systematic shifts were understood the clock reached 10^-18. At that level the clock sees gravitational time dilation over millimetres to centimetres and constrains variations of fundamental constants and ultralight dark matter. That is quantum mechanics of atoms understood to the last digit, which is the kind of result I trust. The attribution is also the cleanest on the list: Katori proposed and first realised the scheme, and Ye's group took it to record accuracy and stability with new many-body clock physics. Several independent laboratories now reproduce and compare clocks at this level, so this is not a single-measurement claim.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that this is a refinement of an area already honoured: the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and the 2012 prize for controlling individual quantum systems, including ion clocks. A committee could read it as engineering progress in precision metrology rather than a new discovery about nature. Credit is also wider than two names, since the Paris, NIST/Boulder and PTB groups made decisive contributions. Finally, the SI second has not yet been redefined, so some members may feel the payoff is still to come. I regard these as real qualifications but not disqualifying.

responses.point: Ulf ranks B001 first but asks whether the committee will see it as a technological refinement of the 2005 comb and 2012 clock prizes, and notes that other clock groups could be argued as decisive.
responses.response: I share the worry but weigh it differently. The comb and the ion-trap prizes honoured the tools and the control of single quantum systems. The lattice clock is a different mechanism: the magic wavelength lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once with the trap perturbation cancelled, which is what makes 10^-18 stability reachable. The resulting measurements, such as time dilation across a millimetre-sized sample, are new observations about nature and not only a better number. On other groups, I agree the Paris and Boulder strontium and ytterbium efforts matter, but Katori's proposal and first realisation and Ye's route to 10^-18 are the two clearly identifiable decisive steps.

responses.point: Mark ranks B001 first but would want the SI redefinition well advanced, and flags overlap with the ion-clock work recognised in 2012.
responses.response: I do not think the Nobel Prize should wait for the redefinition. The physics is confirmed now by many laboratories, and a redefinition is a metrological and political decision that follows the science. Waiting would reward the committee process rather than the discovery. On ion clocks, Wineland's prize was for manipulating single quantum systems, and the most accurate ion clocks use a different physical principle. I accept your point as a reason to word the citation around the optical lattice scheme and not around clocks in general.

responses.point: Eva Olsson puts B015 (tunnel magnetoresistance) first, on the grounds of an original experimental discovery with decisive technological impact and a natural follow-on to the 2007 GMR prize, and ranks B001 second.
responses.response: I respect the maturity and reproducibility of the TMR work, and I agree the 1995 room-temperature observations are real discoveries. My difficulty is attribution: your own ballot notes that the MgO-barrier step belongs partly to groups outside the credited names, such as Yuasa and the Butler and Mathon theory, so any three-person prize risks being incomplete. The technological payoff also counts for less with me than what the discovery tells us about nature, and it follows the GMR prize closely. B001 has a cleaner two-person attribution, so I would keep it ahead, while accepting B015 as a serious alternative if colleagues weigh application heavily.

responses.point: Goran ranks B003 (circuit QED) first and B001 only fifth, noting that B001 is distinct but follows earlier prizes, and he defers to AMO colleagues on it.
responses.response: Taking you at your word, I will say that the field is not a rerun of earlier prizes. The distinction between B001 and the 2025 circuit prize is also useful. B003 is scientifically strong, and I ranked it fifth myself. But the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits was only last year, and four credited names for three places leaves a real allocation problem, with Girvin and Blais competing for one theory slot. You also flag your own programme ties to that community. For those reasons I would not put B003 ahead of B001 this year, although I would not call it a weaker discovery.

responses.point: Stefan ranks B001 first as a step change in measurement precision, and ranks B042 third, with attribution difficulty between theory and experiment.
responses.response: I agree with you on B001, and on your point that precision limits what can be learned. On B042 we differ slightly: I ranked it second and see it as the strongest second option, but you are right that the theory proposal and the experiments need different recognition. Choosing Bloch, Zoller and Greiner leaves out Cirac and Esslinger, and the Mott transition owes something to the earlier BEC prize community. This is why I keep B042 only as an alternative and do not propose a two-part prize with B001.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues treat the lattice clock as a new discovery or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether credit for the strontium lattice clock should be extended beyond Katori and Ye to other groups, which the three-person limit and the supplied names do not allow.
For B042, which three of the five credited names (Bloch, Zoller, Greiner, Esslinger, Cirac) form a defensible prize if the committee prefers it.
I rely on general knowledge, not on a documented priority check, for the early lattice-clock priority record.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with B001 is apparent from my profile. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of the credited names for the shortlisted ballots are among my listed collaborators. I should flag that I work in atomic theory and have collaborated with groups in AMO, which is relevant to B001 and B042 only as a field-level connection.
